title: Around the Loop, and Out of It

scenes.visual: Title card 'Around the Loop, and Out of It' over the farm cutaway, one GREEN dot glowing brighter than the rest. COLOUR MAP (both films): nitrogen gas = GREY PAIRED DOTS (two dots joined by a short bar) filling a big pale-grey sky 'tank'; usable nitrogen = small GREEN DOTS in light-blue soil water; sugar = an ORANGE arrow; the 'gate' = a small glowing GOLD clasp on the bar of every grey pair, holding its two dots together; only changers can snap a clasp open, and then the pair becomes green dots. Grey pairs drift freely everywhere, into soil, around roots and into nodules, still clasped; the gate is the clasp, not a place. Never draw a gate line at the soil surface. Setting: the same Virginia farm cutaway in every scene: soybeans on the left, corn on the right, woods with a white-tailed deer behind, a stream running off to the Chesapeake Bay. Plants, animals and microbes are cartoons; every cutaway is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. No molecular structures. Same colours and gold gate as the first film. The followed atom is drawn with a white halo so it can be tracked.

scenes.tts: Follow one nitrogen atom. Once it is part of a soybean leaf, is it there for good? Or does it keep on moving?
scenes.visual: A soybean leaf on screen; a single haloed dot sits inside it. Question card: 'Once it is in a leaf, is it there for good?'
scenes.narration: Follow one nitrogen atom. Once it is part of a soybean leaf, is it there for good? Or does it keep on moving?

scenes.tts: In the first film, nitrogen gas stayed locked until a changer opened it. Now follow one atom that a nodule changed.
scenes.visual: Quick replay of the first film's shot: grey sky tank of clasped pairs, small green pool, a clasp snapping open inside a nodule. The camera then picks out one haloed atom.
scenes.narration: In the first film, nitrogen gas stayed locked until a changer opened it. Now follow one atom that a nodule changed.

scenes.tts: Here is our atom, one half of a grey pair in the air. A nodule changes it into usable nitrogen. The plant builds it into a protein in a leaf.
scenes.visual: The haloed atom starts as one dot of a clasped grey pair in the sky, drifts down into a nodule, where the clasp snaps open; it turns GREEN, travels up the stem and docks in a labelled 'protein' block inside a leaf.
scenes.narration: Here is our atom, one half of a grey pair in the air. A nodule changes it into usable nitrogen. The plant builds it into a protein in a leaf.

scenes.tts: A white-tailed deer wanders over and eats the leaf. The deer digests the leaf's proteins. Our atom becomes part of a protein in the deer's body. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
scenes.visual: A cartoon white-tailed deer browses the soybean leaf. Cutaway of the deer, labelled 'schematic': the 'protein' block breaks into pieces and the haloed atom rebuilds into a new 'protein' block in the deer's leg.
scenes.narration: A white-tailed deer wanders over and eats the leaf. The deer digests the leaf's proteins. Our atom becomes part of a protein in the deer's body. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.

scenes.tts: Later, the deer dies in the woods. Is its nitrogen gone for good, or not? Pause and decide.
scenes.visual: Seasons change; the deer lies on the forest floor among fallen leaves (drawn gently, not graphic). Pause card: 'Is the deer's nitrogen gone for good?' with buttons 'gone' and 'not gone'. Ring timer.
scenes.narration: Later, the deer dies in the woods. Is its nitrogen gone for good, or not? Pause and decide.

scenes.visual: Pause card holds; ring timer runs down.

scenes.tts: No, it is not gone. Decomposers go to work. A decomposer is a living thing, such as a fungus or a bacterium, that breaks down dead things and wastes.
scenes.visual: White fungus threads spread through the leaf litter and tiny rod-shaped bacteria gather, labelled 'decomposers: fungi and bacteria'. On-screen definition: 'decomposer: breaks down dead things and wastes'.
scenes.narration: No, it is not gone. Decomposers go to work. A decomposer is a living thing, such as a fungus or a bacterium, that breaks down dead things and wastes.

scenes.tts: Decomposers break down the deer's body and its droppings. Our atom returns to the soil as usable nitrogen, one green dot in the soil water.
scenes.visual: The deer outline fades into the soil; droppings nearby fade too. The haloed atom drops into the light-blue soil water as a GREEN dot.
scenes.narration: Decomposers break down the deer's body and its droppings. Our atom returns to the soil as usable nitrogen, one green dot in the soil water.

scenes.tts: A corn root reaches it and takes it up. Same atom, second plant. The corn builds our atom into a brand new protein in one of its leaves.
scenes.visual: A corn root grows toward the haloed green dot and draws it up the stalk into a 'protein' block in a corn leaf. Small label: 'same atom, second plant'.
scenes.narration: A corn root reaches it and takes it up. Same atom, second plant. The corn builds our atom into a brand new protein in one of its leaves.

scenes.tts: Later, the corn plant dies. Decomposers return our atom to the soil as one usable form. In soil with oxygen, other bacteria change it into a second usable form.
scenes.visual: The corn stalk falls; fungus threads and bacteria break it down and the haloed atom drops back into the soil water as a GREEN dot with a small tag 'usable form 1'. The soil around it is crumbly, with small air pockets labelled 'oxygen'. Rod-shaped bacteria labelled 'bacteria that need oxygen, schematic' take in green dots and release them with a new tag 'usable form 2'; the haloed atom's tag changes from 'usable form 1' to 'usable form 2'. No grey pairs form in this scene.
scenes.narration: Later, the corn plant dies. Decomposers return our atom to the soil as one usable form. In soil with oxygen, other bacteria change it into a second usable form.

scenes.tts: Then heavy rain soaks the soil, and little oxygen is left. Different bacteria change that second form back into nitrogen gas. Our atom rises into the air again.
scenes.visual: Rain falls; the patch turns low and waterlogged, the air pockets fill with water and the 'oxygen' labels fade; caption 'soggy soil: little oxygen'. Different bacteria, labelled 'other soil bacteria, schematic', take in only dots tagged 'usable form 2', the haloed one among them, and turn them back into clasped grey pairs, which bubble up out of the soil into the sky tank. Dots tagged 'usable form 1' are never shown turning into gas.
scenes.narration: Then heavy rain soaks the soil, and little oxygen is left. Different bacteria change that second form back into nitrogen gas. Our atom rises into the air again.

scenes.tts: This loop, from the air, through the soil and living things, and back to the air, is the nitrogen cycle. At every step, our atom changed form. It was never made, and never destroyed.
scenes.visual: A circular arrow traces the whole path: sky, nodule, soybean leaf, deer, decomposers, soil, corn, decomposers again, 'usable form 1', soil with oxygen, 'usable form 2', soggy soil, and back to the sky. Label in the middle: 'nitrogen cycle'. Corner counter stays fixed: '1 atom: changed form, never made, never destroyed'.
scenes.narration: This loop, from the air, through the soil and living things, and back to the air, is the nitrogen cycle. At every step, our atom changed form. It was never made, and never destroyed.

scenes.tts: Now a second case. A farmer spreads far more fertilizer than the corn can take up. The pool of green dots fills, and then overflows.
scenes.visual: The fertilizer bag pours green dots onto the cornfield until the light-blue soil pool brims over its edge; corn roots take up only some. Caption: 'more than the corn can take up'.
scenes.narration: Now a second case. A farmer spreads far more fertilizer than the corn can take up. The pool of green dots fills, and then overflows.

scenes.tts: Then a heavy rain falls. Water moving over and through the soil carries the extra green dots into a stream. The stream flows toward the Chesapeake Bay.
scenes.visual: Rain falls; blue arrows run across the surface and down through the soil, sweeping green dots into the stream. Follow the stream on a simple map arrow toward a label 'Chesapeake Bay'.
scenes.narration: Then a heavy rain falls. Water moving over and through the soil carries the extra green dots into a stream. The stream flows toward the Chesapeake Bay.

scenes.tts: In the Bay, the extra nitrogen feeds an algal bloom, a fast growth of algae in the water. The water near the surface turns thick and green.
scenes.visual: Bay surface, side view labelled 'schematic': green dots arrive and tiny algae multiply quickly until the top layer is thick green. Label 'algal bloom'. Stop here: no dying algae, no fish shown.
scenes.narration: In the Bay, the extra nitrogen feeds an algal bloom, a fast growth of algae in the water. The water near the surface turns thick and green.

scenes.tts: So nitrogen goes around the loop, changing form, and is never used up. But water can carry it out of a field, and into the Bay.
scenes.visual: Return to the circular loop arrow over the farm. A side branch arrow, blue, leaks from the soil pool down the stream to the Bay. Caption: 'never used up, but it can leave a field'.
scenes.narration: So nitrogen goes around the loop, changing form, and is never used up. But water can carry it out of a field, and into the Bay.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line: 'Nitrogen changes form around the loop but is never used up.'
